text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
English religious leader JOHN WESLEY, who founded Methodism, was born in 1703.

Grazier and explorer GREGORY BLAXLAND, who was also one of our earliest wine-makers, was born in 1778. He petitioned the government for huge land grants, but was unsuccessful, and eventually committed suicide.
French composer CHARLES GOUNOD, whose most successful works were the operas "Faust" and "Romeo And Juliet", was born in 1818.

Australian engineer JOHN FURPHY was born in 1842. He built horsedrawn iron-tank watercarts, and the word "furphy" became synonymous with gossip because cart drivers were generally renowned for their ability to 'stretch the truth' and tell 'tall tales'. Workers and in WW I, Diggers, gathered around the Furphy watercarts to swap rumours. His brother JOSEPH was also a teller of tales and wrote under the name of TOM COLLINS. That name too
was used as an expression to describe exaggerated stories.
Writer and poet HENRY LAWSON, described as the 'first articulate voice of the real Australian, was born in 1867.

American singer/actor DEAN MARTIN (DINO CROCETTI), who first teamed up with comedian JERRY LEWIS at a club in Atlanta in 1946, was born in 1917. On top of a successful singing and acting career, he also had his own television show in the United States from 1965 until 1974. (His birthday is also quoted as the 7th of June).

American singer/songwriter BARRY MANILOW (BARRY ALLAN PINKUS), whose career started as a jingle writer (he penned the McDonald slogan 'You deserve a break today'), was born in 1946. His biggest hits were "Mandy" (1974/75) and "I Write The Songs" (1975).
** EVENTS **
656 : Caliph UTHMAN, third caliph to rule after the
death of the Prophet, was assassinated at his home in Medina (now Saudi Arabia) by besieging Moslem rebels from Mesopotamia.
1579 : FRANCIS DRAKE dropped the Golden Hind's anchor off
the south-west coast of America (California), and named the area 'New Albion'.
1775 : In the American War of Independence, British
forces defeated the Americans at the Battle of Bunker Hill which took place at Breed's Hill near Boston. The British won at the cost of 800 out of their force of 2,000.
1823 : CHARLES MACINTOSH patented a waterproof material,
useful in the making of clothing to protect against rain.
1867 : JOSEPH LISTER made the first attempt of any form
of antiseptic treatment, performing a mastectomy upon his sister in Glasgow Royal Infirmary, using carbolic acid as an antiseptic.
1939 : The last person to be publicly guillotined in
France, murderer EUGEN WEIDMANN, was executed before a large crowd at Versailles.
1944 : Iceland became an independent republic.
1950 : The first kidney transplant was performed, in
Chicago.
1963 : Russian cosmonuts VALENTINA TERESHKOVA and Colonel
VALERY BYKOVSKY liased for the world's first ever date in space. Their Vostok craft were in orbit above the earth, just 12 seconds apart.
1967 : China exploded its first hydrogen bomb.
1970 : EDWIN LAND patented the first Polaroid camera.
1972 : Five men were caught snoopping around the

Washington headquarters of the United States Democratic Party, in the Watergate Hotel. All were equipped with electronic eavesdropping equipment, and were rumoured to have been on the payroll of the "Republican Committee for the Re-election of the President", a group known as 'CREEP'. The resulting scandal led to the resignation of President RICHARD NIXON.
1982 : In Argentina, General LEOPOLDO GALTIERI resigned
as president following the country's defeat in the Falklands War.
1982 : Italian ROBERTO CALVI, a central figure in the

Banca Ambrosiano scandal that was rocking the country, was found hanging under Blackfriars Bridge in London. His pockets had been weighed down with bricks and stones, and he had $20,000 in cash on him. The President of the Vatican Bank, Archbishop MARCINKUS, had also been implicated in the scandal.
1988 : Jamaican poet DENNIS LOBAN was found guilty of
murdering reggae star PETER TOSH and was sentenced to hang.
1991 : Eight thousand scientists and researchers gathered
at Fortezza da Basso in Florence, for a major international conference on AIDS. By this time the virus had spread to 163 countries, and was rife in Africa.
1991 : South Africa's white-dominated parliament voted to
end race classification, the legal foundation of apartheid since 1950.
1994 : American football star O.J. SIMPSON, accused of
killing his ex-wife and a male friend, was arrested after a dramatic motorway chase and a 90-minute standoff in the driveway of his estate.
